TRIP alloys, this work provides a novel way to develop super-

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: This work provides interesting results concerning radiation tolerance improvements via surface treatment. The ion irradiation is an acceptable starting point for further investigation of radiation effects in this unique microstructure. Generally the conclusions are supported by the data, and the experimental and computation methods are sound. However, additional detail and explanation of certain concepts is suggested. This work is recommended for minor revision, then publication pending that revision.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be addressed.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect, shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
2. The manuscript claims that the AMT mechanism is related to high-density SFs. So, what is the value of it. A detailed value would be appreciated.
3. The authors focus on studying the microstructure of the peak damage region. According to the dose and ion distribution map provided in Supplementary Fig. 3, the irradiation dose and ion concentration in the peak damage area are much higher than other irradiation regions. So, will this affect the martensitic transformation in this work?
4. In lines 105-106, the authors mention a 3D dislocation network was formed in 304NG by SMRT. That’s interesting. However, there seems to be no experimental evidence, and only been demonstrated through MD simulations.
5. In lines 141-143, “it is interesting to notice that both the density and size of DLs significantly decrease……0.5 to 5 dpa……” the range of the dose is incorrect (refer to Supplementary Fig. 4).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript states the radiation tolerance of metals can be enhanced by a mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation. The manuscript uses the experimental methods and molecular dynamics simulations to reveal this mechanism. After reviewing this manuscript, the reviewer has some comments. See details in below.
1. Is the first paragraph the abstract? If this is an abstract, we should not cite the references. Please remove these references and reorganize the references in the whole manuscript.
2.This manuscript is comparing the radiation behaviors of the CG and GNS material, I would suggest revealing the grain size distribution for both CG and GNS. The manuscript only listed the average grain size of CG is 26 µm, what is the grain size and its distribution for GNS?
3.This manuscript discussed the phase transformation under irradiations. What about the radiation induced grain growth, especially under the high dose after 155 dpa? The authors should also reveal the grain size after 155 dpa and explain why the material is still within nanometer scale after high irradiation dose in more details. I can see the authors mentioned combining low energy interfaces, SFs, and DNs contributes to a high stability from both thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives. Please explain more how these interfaces, SFs and DNs will contribute the structure stability in thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives.
4. I suggest all the SAED patterns in this manuscript should be identified. Especially the diffraction rings for the martensite in the GNS images.
5.In Figure 2, this manuscript is discussing the DL size of the CG and GNS sample. However, the error bar for the CG sample is way bigger than the GNS sample. Can you explain this?
6.Based on the discussion and Figure 2, it looks like after 10 dpa, the DL size and density remain flat. Please explain why 10 dpa is the critical irradiation point in more details? Why will the DL size not increase, and DL density will not decrease after 10 dpa? Is this related to the martensitic phase?
7. Please check all the references and keep them in the same format. Especially the format for the journal’s name.
8. In extended data figure 3, why did not put the images for 155 dpa? It only includes the images up to 85 dpa. Since 155 dpa is the final dose, I would suggest adding the images for 155 dpa.
9. In extended data figure 4, the figure 4 (b) has no scale bar. Also, it looks larger of the DL in Figure d than Figure c. Please clarify this.
10. In extended data figure 6, it says the white arrows show g= [001]. However, it is very difficult to see in the images, please improve the image quality.
11. In the supplementary Figure 3, I would suggest changing the curve colors in the right image to make it more obvious to see the difference.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response-to-Reviewers:
Manuscript ID: NCOMMS-25-38174-T
Title: Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic
Transformation
Authors: S. Zhang et al.
The authors would like to thank all the reviewers for the valuable comments and
suggestions which are definitely helpful for making the manuscript more accurate and
clearer. According to the comments and suggestions, we have performed some
additional works (including some new experiments, e.g. see the replies to Reviewer 2:
Comment 1; Reviewer 3: Comment 9), and expanded the introduction and discussion
(including the TRIP effect, see the reply to Reviewer 2: Comment 1). And we have
revised the manuscript accordingly, as highlighted in yellow in the revised manuscript.
Below detailed responses to the comments are listed.
Reviewer #1:
This work provides interesting results concerning radiation tolerance improvements via
surface treatment. The ion irradiation is an acceptable starting point for further
investigation of radiation effects in this unique microstructure. Generally the
conclusions are supported by the data, and the experimental and computation methods
are sound. However, additional detail and explanation of certain concepts is suggested.
This work is recommended for minor revision, then publication pending that revision.
REPLY：Thanks for your insightful comments and constructive suggestions!
1) P2 Line 67: What is the different between gradient nanostructured material and
severe plastic deformation at the surface of the material?
REPLY: In this work, we used a surface severe plastic deformation method, surface
mechanical rolling treatment (SMRT), to produce gradient nanostructured 304NG.
From this aspect, SMRT is a method implementing severe plastic deformation at the
surface of materials. However, higher strain and strain rates are typically required at the
 at the
material surface in SMRT than that in conventional severe plastic deformation methods
[1, 2] to achieve gradient nanostructures, as revealed in Ref. [3]. Moreover, SMRT
shows advantages of low cost and high flexibility in processing large-sized components
compared to conventional severe plastic deformation methods such as equal channel
angular pressing [1] and high-pressure torsion [2]. Meanwhile, in addition to surface
severe plastic deformation methods, some other methods, such as electro-deposition [4]
and magnetron sputtering [5], can also be applied to produce GNS materials.
Following your question, the difference between gradient nanostructured material and
severe plastic deformation at material surface has been mentioned in the revised
manuscript (P14 Lines 390-395).
2. P3 Line 74: What is the reason that 304 specifically was chosen for this study? What
would the best application of this technique in reactor be? Is it more advantageous to
a component which received a high dose rate, or one that receives dose, but is more
affected by temperature?
REPLY: Mostly due to its outstanding performance of mechanical properties, high-
temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, and acceptable radiation resistance, 304
stainless steel has been applied for decades as the primary components in pressured
water reactors (PWR) and boiling water reactors (BWR) [6]. For example, this material
has been used as the core structures, primary pipes, pump materials and so on in PWRs,
and used as plates of core shroud, core supporting structures, pipes in jet pumps and so
on in BWRs. Furthermore, 304 stainless steel has also been considered as a main
structural material in both nuclear fusion reactors [7] and next-generation reactors [8].
To understand and improve their radiation resistance would thus be useful and
necessary for the current and future nuclear reactors. Therefore, we selected 304
stainless steel in this work, to further improve its resistance to radiation damage.
SMRT and the AMT mechanism can be applied on pipes and plates of 304 stainless
steel in reactors as mentioned above.
According to the present results, the AMT mechanism in GNS-304 NG can be applied
after high dose radiation, e.g. up to 150 dpa. In fact, the radiation dose rate in ion-
implantation experiments was also high (up to 2.7810-4 dpa s-1) in this work. Thus,
this mechanism can also work for cases under a high radiation dose rate. As for the
temperature effect, we have proved that this mechanism still works well at temperature
up to 450 C, while beyond which no experiments have been performed at present.
Therefore, the AMT mechanism should have advantageous to a component which
receives a high dose and/or a high dose rate at temperatures at least up to 450 C.
In the revised manuscript, the reason that 304 stainless steel was chosen has been added
in P3 Lines 80-82, and the application possibilities of SMRT and AMT mechanism have
been further discussed in P13 Line 372-374.
3. P6: Line 144: The difference in loop size and density evolution could be understood
in the context of faulted loop growth and unfaulting, which could lead to decreasing
loop size
REPLY: Yes. The evolution from faulted loops (e.g. 1/3<111> loops in austenite)
before martensitic transformation to unfaulted loops (e.g. 1/2<111> loops in martensite)
after martensitic transformation can be used to understand the difference in loop size
and density evolution in this work, especially for the decrease of loop size shown in
Fig. 2c.
From Fig. 2, Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 7 (in the revised manuscript, hereafter the
same), one can see that before martensitic transformation dominates the defect
evolution process (e.g. at doses below 2 dpa), the faulted 1/3<111> loops are primary
interstitial cluster defects in FCC austenite, which have low diffusion capability [9] and
their average size could increase through absorption of interstitials induced by
displacement cascades. When the martensitic transformation dominates the defect
evolution process (e.g. at doses larger than around 2 dpa), the formed loops in the
transformed martensitic phase (BCC) are unfaulted 1/2<111> loops with very low
diffusion energy barrier [9], resulting in their fast absorption by a high density of grain
boundaries, dislocation networks and stacking faults, which would also absorb the
radiation induced point defects. Meanwhile, the AMT mechanism further annihilates
the point defects, resulting in a decreasing number of interstitials to be absorbed by
dislocation loops. Thus, the average loop size decreases, as shown in Fig. 2c.
Corresponding changes have been made in the revised manuscript (P6 Lines 152-154).
Fig. R1. Variations of DLs density and size with radiation dose at room temperature in
CG and GNS samples. This is an enlarged view of Fig. 2c showing the situation at low
doses.
4. P6 Line 160: What reactor system is T91 currently being used in?
REPLY: T91 steel is widely used as structural material in nuclear reactors mostly
because of its high mechanical properties, good phase stability, reduced activity, and
high resistance to stress corrosion cracking. For example, in current fission reactors,
T91 is used to manufacture pressure vessels, piping systems, and power boilers [10-12].
In the sodium-cooled and lead-cooled fast fission reactors, T91 has also been selected
as a candidate for fuel cladding, duct/wrapper, and structural materials [13, 14].
Furthermore, it is also an important candidate for structural components in future fusion
power reactors [15] and concentrated solar power plants [16]. And T91 steel has also
been considered as a candidate structural material in accelerator-driven subcritical
system (ADS) served for nuclear reactors [17].
The applications of T91 steel in current reactor systems have been mentioned in the
revised manuscript (see P6 lines 172-173).
5. P6: Line 167: Any comment on by which mechanism the voids are suppressed in GNS
components?
REPLY: In GNS components, two mechanisms could accelerate the annihilation of
radiation-induced displacement damages (mostly vacancies, interstitials, and their
small clusters), and therefore suppress the formation of voids (recombined vacancies
and small vacancy cluster) during the radiation process at high temperatures. The 1st
one is the absorption of vacancies and small vacancy clusters by a high density of grain
boundaries, dislocation networks and stacking faults. Compared to state in normal
nanocrystal samples, the density of above mentioned structures (grain boundaries,
dislocation networks and stacking faults) in GNS is much higher, which could result in
high probability for them to interact with their surrounding point defects (e.g. interstitial,
vacancies and small defect clusters) induced by displacement cascade. Thus, the total
number of left vacancies and small vacancy clusters should be lower than that in normal
nanocrystal samples and CG samples. Furthermore, at low temperatures (e.g. less than
300 ℃), diffusion of vacancies and their clusters is limited, thus, the formation of voids
through absorption of these left vacancy defects has been suppressed. It should be noted
that while the microstructure remains stable after irradiation at 450 C, this mechanism
still works in GNS samples. The 2nd one to suppress formation of void is related to the
AMT process explored in this work, which would annihilate the vacancies and small
vacancy clusters by lattice rearrangement during the AMT process, as revealed by the
present MD simulation results (Supplementary Video 4). Therefore, the total number of
vacancies and small vacancy clusters in both austenite and the transformed martensite
to form a void is further decreased by AMT process.
The mechanisms by which the radiation resistance is enhanced in GNS components
have been analyzed in detail in Section Anti-radiation mechanisms. And some revisions
have been made to make the analysis more accurate and clearer in the revised
manuscript (P6 Line 177; P7 Lines 201-203; P8 Lines 235-237).
6. P6 Line 171-174: These sentences are in contradiction to one another. Is refined
microstructure an enhancement or an Achilles heel to radiation resistance? Radiation
resistance should be understood in the context of defect sinks, while refined
microstructure propensity for grain growth can be understood in the context of stored
energy within the microstructure.
REPLY: Sorry that these sentences are not precise and bring misunderstanding. In fact,
the refined microstructure provides a high density of grain boundaries, which absorbs
radiation defects and significantly increases the radiation resistance. However, this
mechanism can only work well when the grain size is kept in the nanometer scale. When
a large number of radiation defects has been absorbed by nanostructured materials
under irradiation, the diffusion of grain boundaries would occur, which results in
Ostwald ripening process and finally leads to the instability of refined microstructure
as reported previously [18, 19]. At this stage, these materials are not with refined
microstructures and thus don’t show significantly enhanced radiation resistance
anymore.
Corresponding corrections have been made to avoid misunderstandings in the revised
manuscript. As shown in P7 Lines 184-189, the sentences have been changed to “One
should be its specific nanostructures with a high stability. Conventionally, refining
microstructure leads to an enhanced radiation resistance, mostly due to the existence of
numerous GBs acting as sinks of radiation induced defects. However, the instability of
refined microstructure is an Achilles heel of traditional NC materials under irradiation,
mostly due to the high stored energy of GBs in them”.
7. P7 Line 201: By what mechanism does the martensitic transformation occur directly
from irradiation? What is the driving force in the absence of a mechanical load to
initiate the transformation?
REPLY: According to the results of high-resolution STEM observations and MD
simulations, we inferred that the martensitic transformation occurs mostly due to the
interactions between pre-existing SFs and radiation-induced defects in irradiated GNS
304NG. As shown in Figs. 3(b, c) and Supplementary Fig. 21(c, d) in the revised
manuscript, the martensitic phase transition occurs mainly at the junctions of SFs after
irradiation, which conforms to the classical Kurdjumov-Sachs relationship. And further
MD simulations indicated that the phase transition is initiated while the radiation-
induced defects are absorbed by the SFs (Supplementary Video 4), confirming that the
radiation induced phase transformation is firstly induced by the interaction between SFs
and radiation-induced defects. And the mechanism of large-scale AMT was also
analyzed by building a MD model (Supplementary Fig. 25a) with cross SFs around the
newly formed martensite phase. Under the interaction of SFs and radiation-induced
defects, the phenomenon that martensite extends along these interactions to both sides
(Supplementary Fig. 25b, Supplementary Video 5) is confirmed. By analyzing the
displacement of interstitial atoms, it is found that the displacement of defects near the
interface between SFs and martensite is more significant, and finally martensite occurs
at the intersection of SFs and extends to both sides (Supplementary Fig. 25c).
Meanwhile, the corresponding phase transformation also promotes atomic
displacements after the formation of new martensite phase, resulting in continuous
martensitic transformation and related defect absorption from the damage peak to the
surrounding regions.
It is noted that the application of external stress is just to accelerate the phase
transformation process without affecting the underlying mechanism during MD
simulations in this work, although inhomogeneous stress fields do exist in irradiated
samples induced by implantation of energetic particles [20]. For example, a previous
study [20] demonstrated that the ion implantation could result in concentration gradient
and stress fields in the near-surface layer, and the maximum value could reach several
hundred MPa. Furthermore, displacement cascades and the formation of radiation
defects would also induce inhomogeneous stress fields around these regions [21].
Correspondingly, the driving force of martensitic transformation in irradiated GNS
samples mostly comes from the excess free energies relating with the pre-existing SFs
and radiation-induced defects. Meanwhile, the residual stresses introduced by SMRT,
phase transition, chemical segregation under irradiation and energetic particle
irradiation, might also provide additional driving force. And their contributions have
been discussed in the manuscript (see P10 Lines 273-277, Lines 302-307).
Some other changes have also been made to further clarify the AMT mechanism in the
revised manuscript (see P10 Lines 273-274, Lines 280-284, and Supplementary Note
1).
8. P8 Line 218: What does adaptive martensitic transformation mean, and how is this
different from a standard martensitic transformation?
REPLY: According to experimental and simulative results in this work, we found that
the martensitic transformation in irradiated GNS 304NG samples occurs much faster
and in a broader region than that a standard martensitic transformation in irradiated
coarse-grained counterparts. Therefore, we proposed the adaptive martensitic
transformation (AMT) to name the martensitic transformation process in GNS samples
under irradiation.
In detail, the AMT mechanism shows different features from the standard martensitic
transformation: 1) The AMT completes in a much lower dose in the peak damage region
of GNS samples than a standard martensitic transformation under irradiation at room
temperature without the application of external stress. The AMT results in a full
distribution of martensite in the peak damage region after irradiation at 12 dpa; while a
large fraction of austenite retains in the peak damage region after a standard martensitic
transformation even at 155 dpa. 2) The AMT progresses adaptively from the peak
damage region to the surrounding regions; while a standard martensitic transformation
occurs only in the peak damage region. 3) The AMT can occur at high temperatures
(e.g. 450 C) when no standard martensitic transformation can occur.
Corresponding changes have been made in the revised manuscript (P8 Line 221; Lines
240-243).
9. P9 Line 247: These stacking faults group together to form an hcp metastable
martensitic phase, which should be observable in the sample.
REPLY: Yes. HCP metastable martensitic phase (-martensite) can be formed by
overlapping bundles of stacking faults on {111} planes in principle, so that -martensite
should be observed in irradiated samples. However, we haven’t detected the formation
of -martensite in irradiated samples by TEM observations and XRD analyses in this
work.
Following the comment of the referee, we carefully checked the FFT pattern in Fig. 3c
in the manuscript (also shown in Fig. R2 here). It should be emphasized that this is an
image observed at the 1 nm scale in a grain. At the atomic scale (i.e. HRTEM or
HRSTEM), although it is possible that the misarrangement of continuous two or more
atomic layers (as marked by orange dash lines in Fig. R2a) might introduce the
diffraction spots of HCP phase in corresponding FFT patterns in FCC metals, more
analyses are required to confirm this possibility since the FFT patterns only reflect the
periodic changes in atomic lattice arrangement. In this work, it can be determined that
the misarrangement layers are SFs rather than HCP metastable phases according to the
diffraction pattern theory, as explained below: Firstly, the diffraction spots of γ and α'-
martensite can be easily identified (marked by red and green, respectively, in Fig. R2b).
Secondly, according to the lattice constants of ε-martensite (a = b = 2.53 Å, c = 4.12
Å), a spot which seems to match the (101̅0)𝜀 should be observed (circled in orange
in Fig. R2b). However, the D of the spot is 8.15 nm-1, while the calculated value of
𝐷 = 9.13 nm-1 (error > 10%). The possibility that this diffraction spot is from -
(101̅0)𝜀
martensite should be excluded. Therefore, the bundles should still be SFs, and the
formation of an HCP phase by overlapping SFs bundles, within a thickness less than
0.5 nm, should be excluded in this figure.
However, further investigations are expected to reveal the formation of metastable -
martensite in irradiated samples, especially with the contribution from SFs.
This point has been explained in the revised manuscript (P10 Lines 284-287).
Fig. R2. (also Fig. 3c in the manuscript) The transformation in the lattice arrangement
from  to  phase at SFs in GNS 304NG under irradiation at 2 dpa. a, A high-resolution
STEM image. b, The FFT pattern of (a) with marks showing the diffraction spots of ,
’, and expected  phases.
10. P9 Line 258: If this were to be the case, then once the MT was complete you would
expect to see an increase in the DL size and density
REPLY: Yes. The DL size and density should increase after the completion of MT.
According to the proposed AMT mechanism in this work, the radiation resistance
should be significantly enhanced due to lattice rearrangement during the AMT. When
the AMT is not complete, the surrounding regions under AMT will be strong sinks for
radiation-induced defects, which should result in a lower DL size and density. When
the AMT is complete, no such a mechanism processes in the radiation affected range
anymore, so that the DL size and density is expected to increase. It is noted that the
formed BCC martensitic phase should be more radiation resistant than the original FCC
austenitic phase, so that there should be a balance between an enhancing radiation
resistance (due to increasing martensite fraction) and a decreasing resistance (due to
reducing AMT ability) with an increasing radiation dose. As demonstrated in
Supplementary Fig. 15 in the revised manuscript, in comparison with the DL density in
GNS 304 counterparts possessing a similar grain size distribution but much more pre-
existing martensite (near 100%), an enhanced irradiation resistance can only be
observed in GNS 304NG samples at peak doses > 6 dpa, when a large fraction of
martensite has been formed and the AMT mechanism is still active. No increase in the
DL size and density was observed in irradiated GNS 304NG in Fig. 2c possibly due to
that the AMT is not complete even after irradiation at a peak dose of 155 dpa (see Fig.
3a) in this work.
Corresponding modifications have been made in the revised manuscript (P10 Lines
290-294).

The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic
Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation
demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and
voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. 
Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive
martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And
they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they
also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the
mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed
nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In
the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be
addressed.
REPLY：Thank you for the positive comments and insightful suggestions.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect,
shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the
martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual
stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT
mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a
means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between
martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
REPLY: Yes. We have analyzed the relationship between martensitic transformation
and residual stress in GNS samples under irradiation in this work.
Residual stress might play an important role in martensitic transformation in austenitic
steels, TRIP steels, shape memory alloys, et al. Typically, compressive stresses promote
martensitic transformation by decreasing the energy barrier of transformation. Since
higher compressive residual stresses exist in SMRT 304NG samples than in CG
samples, the AMT process might be further promoted in addition to the contribution of
SFs in GNS samples under irradiation at room temperature. In this work, the role of
residual stress on martensitic transformation has also been revealed by MD simulations,
in which remarkable stresses were introduced so that the martensitic transformation was
accelerated in an austenitic unit (see Supplementary Fig. 21). Meanwhile, it is noticed
that the large-scale AMT and enhanced irradiation resistance have also been observed
in GNS sample irradiated at higher temperatures (see Supplementary Fig. 10), when the
residual stresses are almost completely released. Therefore, it should be SFs play the
dominant role in the AMT process in this work. However, further investigations are
expected to clarify the effect of residual stress on the AMT under irradiation at room
temperature.
Meanwhile, we have measured the residual stresses in the surface layer of GNS and CG
samples before and after irradiation at room temperature. As shown in Fig. R4, a certain
amount of compressive stress was introduced into the surface layer of 304NG samples
by SMRT. As the AMT progresses, the residual compressive stress was further
increased (from -131.215.4 MPa to -182.610.7 MPa), while there is no detectable
change in the residual stress in irradiated CG counterparts.
In addition, as pointed by the reviewer, martensitic transformation is also an issue
relating with TRIP (transformation induced plasticity) effect, and therefore radiation
might bring significant changes in TRIP materials. For example, Agrawal et al. [1]
found that radiation might initiate a self-healing mechanism in TRIP high entropy alloys
(HEAs) by balancing radiation induced martensitic transformation with temperature
induced reverse transformation, so that a high stability of mechanical properties is
achieved in HEAs under irradiation at high doses and temperatures. And the self-
healing mechanism might be introduced to expand the service dose and temperature of
TRIP HEAs in future reactors.
Corresponding modifications have been made in the revised manuscript (P10 Lines
302-307 on residual stress; P2 Lines 65-69, P9 Line 268 and P13 Line 376 on TRIP
effect).

the peak damage region to the surrounding regions until the phase transformation is
completely finished. It should be noted that the surrounding regions around the peak
damage region have different irradiation doses and implanted ion concentrations.
However, the AMT also occurs in these regions. Therefore, it can be known that the
different irradiation doses and ion concentrations have no or slight effects on the
occurrence of AMT process. It should also be noted that the ions used in this work is
Fe-ions, which become Fe atoms and may not affect the formation of DLs and voids in
irradiated 304NG.

304NG by SMRT. That’s interesting. However, there seems to be no experimental

through the interface, and when numerous dislocation lines intertwining with each other,
a dislocation network has been formed in the whole GNS surface region. This
dislocation network structure is thus distributed in both grains and interfaces, forming
a special dislocation structure in GNS materials, as demonstrated in previous studies
[2]. Furthermore, such a DN structure is essentially a type of GNDs, because it is
generated to accommodate strain gradient induced by microstructure gradients.
The dislocation lines which forming DNs have been marked in Fig. 1d and
corresponding changes (see P4 Line 113) have been made in the revised manuscript.

phase transformation has been finished in the whole damage region. Thus, as the referee

### Reviewer 1

This work provides interesting results concerning radiation tolerance improvements via surface treatment. The ion irradiation is an acceptable starting point for further investigation of radiation effects in this unique microstructure. Generally the conclusions are supported by the data, and the experimental and computation methods are sound. However, additional detail and explanation of certain concepts is suggested. This work is recommended for minor revision, then publication pending that revision.

### Reviewer 2

The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be addressed.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect, shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
2. The manuscript claims that the AMT mechanism is related to high-density SFs. So, what is the value of it. A detailed value would be appreciated.
3. The authors focus on studying the microstructure of the peak damage region. According to the dose and ion distribution map provided in Supplementary Fig. 3, the irradiation dose and ion concentration in the peak damage area are much higher than other irradiation regions. So, will this affect the martensitic transformation in this work?
4. In lines 105-106, the authors mention a 3D dislocation network was formed in 304NG by SMRT. That’s interesting. However, there seems to be no experimental evidence, and only been demonstrated through MD simulations.
5. In lines 141-143, “it is interesting to notice that both the density and size of DLs significantly decrease……0.5 to 5 dpa……” the range of the dose is incorrect (refer to Supplementary Fig. 4).

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript states the radiation tolerance of metals can be enhanced by a mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation. The manuscript uses the experimental methods and molecular dynamics simulations to reveal this mechanism. After reviewing this manuscript, the reviewer has some comments. See details in below.
1. Is the first paragraph the abstract? If this is an abstract, we should not cite the references. Please remove these references and reorganize the references in the whole manuscript.
2.This manuscript is comparing the radiation behaviors of the CG and GNS material, I would suggest revealing the grain size distribution for both CG and GNS. The manuscript only listed the average grain size of CG is 26 µm, what is the grain size and its distribution for GNS?
3.This manuscript discussed the phase transformation under irradiations. What about the radiation induced grain growth, especially under the high dose after 155 dpa? The authors should also reveal the grain size after 155 dpa and explain why the material is still within nanometer scale after high irradiation dose in more details. I can see the authors mentioned combining low energy interfaces, SFs, and DNs contributes to a high stability from both thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives. Please explain more how these interfaces, SFs and DNs will contribute the structure stability in thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives.
4. I suggest all the SAED patterns in this manuscript should be identified. Especially the diffraction rings for the martensite in the GNS images.
5.In Figure 2, this manuscript is discussing the DL size of the CG and GNS sample. However, the error bar for the CG sample is way bigger than the GNS sample. Can you explain this?

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This work provides interesting results concerning radiation tolerance improvements via surface treatment. The ion irradiation is an acceptable starting point for further investigation of radiation effects in this unique microstructure. Generally the conclusions are supported by the data, and the experimental and computation methods are sound. However, additional detail and explanation of certain concepts is suggested. This work is recommended for minor revision, then publication pending that revision.

### Reviewer 2

The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be addressed.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect, shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
2. The manuscript claims that the AMT mechanism is related to high-density SFs. So, what is the value of it. A detailed value would be appreciated.
3. The authors focus on studying the microstructure of the peak damage region. According to the dose and ion distribution map provided in Supplementary Fig. 3, the irradiation dose and ion concentration in the peak damage area are much higher than other irradiation regions. So, will this affect the martensitic transformation in this work?
4. In lines 105-106, the authors mention a 3D dislocation network was formed in 304NG by SMRT. That’s interesting. However, there seems to be no experimental evidence, and only been demonstrated through MD simulations.
5. In lines 141-143, “it is interesting to notice that both the density and size of DLs significantly decrease……0.5 to 5 dpa……” the range of the dose is incorrect (refer to Supplementary Fig. 4).

2. P3 Line 74: What is the reason that 304 specifically was chosen for this study? What

REPLY: Mostly due to its outstanding performance of mechanical properties, high-
temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, and acceptable radiation resistance, 304
stainless steel has been applied for decades as the primary components in pressured
water reactors (PWR) and boiling water reactors (BWR) [6]. For example, this material
has been used as the core structures, primary pipes, pump materials and so on in PWRs,
and used as plates of core shroud, core supporting structures, pipes in jet pumps and so
on in BWRs. Furthermore, 304 stainless steel has also been considered as a main
structural material in both nuclear fusion reactors [7] and next-generation reactors [8].
To understand and improve their radiation resistance would thus be useful and
necessary for the current and future nuclear reactors. Therefore, we selected 304
stainless steel in this work, to further improve its resistance to radiation damage.
SMRT and the AMT mechanism can be applied on pipes and plates of 304 stainless
steel in reactors as mentioned above.
According to the present results, the AMT mechanism in GNS-304 NG can be applied
after high dose radiation, e.g. up to 150 dpa. In fact, the radiation dose rate in ion-
implantation experiments was also high (up to 2.7810-4 dpa s-1) in this work. Thus,
this mechanism can also work for cases under a high radiation dose rate. As for the
temperature effect, we have proved that this mechanism still works well at temperature
up to 450 C, while beyond which no experiments have been performed at present.
Therefore, the AMT mechanism should have advantageous to a component which
receives a high dose and/or a high dose rate at temperatures at least up to 450 C.
In the revised manuscript, the reason that 304 stainless steel was chosen has been added

3. P6: Line 144: The difference in loop size and density evolution could be understood
in the context of faulted loop growth and unfaulting, which could lead to decreasing

REPLY: Yes. The evolution from faulted loops (e.g. 1/3<111> loops in austenite)
before martensitic transformation to unfaulted loops (e.g. 1/2<111> loops in martensite)
after martensitic transformation can be used to understand the difference in loop size
and density evolution in this work, especially for the decrease of loop size shown in
Fig. 2c.
From Fig. 2, Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 7 (in the revised manuscript, hereafter the
same), one can see that before martensitic transformation dominates the defect
evolution process (e.g. at doses below 2 dpa), the faulted 1/3<111> loops are primary
interstitial cluster defects in FCC austenite, which have low diffusion capability [9] and
their average size could increase through absorption of interstitials induced by
displacement cascades. When the martensitic transformation dominates the defect
evolution process (e.g. at doses larger than around 2 dpa), the formed loops in the
transformed martensitic phase (BCC) are unfaulted 1/2<111> loops with very low
diffusion energy barrier [9], resulting in their fast absorption by a high density of grain
boundaries, dislocation networks and stacking faults, which would also absorb the
radiation induced point defects. Meanwhile, the AMT mechanism further annihilates
the point defects, resulting in a decreasing number of interstitials to be absorbed by
dislocation loops. Thus, the average loop size decreases, as shown in Fig. 2c.
Corresponding changes have been made in the revised manuscript (P6 Lines 152-154).

5. P6: Line 167: Any comment on by which mechanism the voids are suppressed in GNS

REPLY: In GNS components, two mechanisms could accelerate the annihilation of
radiation-induced displacement damages (mostly vacancies, interstitials, and their
small clusters), and therefore suppress the formation of voids (recombined vacancies
and small vacancy cluster) during the radiation process at high temperatures. The 1st
one is the absorption of vacancies and small vacancy clusters by a high density of grain
boundaries, dislocation networks and stacking faults. Compared to state in normal
nanocrystal samples, the density of above mentioned structures (grain boundaries,
dislocation networks and stacking faults) in GNS is much higher, which could result in
high probability for them to interact with their surrounding point defects (e.g. interstitial,
vacancies and small defect clusters) induced by displacement cascade. Thus, the total
number of left vacancies and small vacancy clusters should be lower than that in normal
nanocrystal samples and CG samples. Furthermore, at low temperatures (e.g. less than
300 ℃), diffusion of vacancies and their clusters is limited, thus, the formation of voids
through absorption of these left vacancy defects has been suppressed. It should be noted
that while the microstructure remains stable after irradiation at 450 C, this mechanism
still works in GNS samples. The 2nd one to suppress formation of void is related to the
AMT process explored in this work, which would annihilate the vacancies and small
vacancy clusters by lattice rearrangement during the AMT process, as revealed by the
present MD simulation results (Supplementary Video 4). Therefore, the total number of
vacancies and small vacancy clusters in both austenite and the transformed martensite
to form a void is further decreased by AMT process.

should be its specific nanostructures with a high stability. Conventionally, refining
microstructure leads to an enhanced radiation resistance, mostly due to the existence of
numerous GBs acting as sinks of radiation induced defects. However, the instability of
refined microstructure is an Achilles heel of traditional NC materials under irradiation,
mostly due to the high stored energy of GBs in them”.
7. P7 Line 201: By what mechanism does the martensitic transformation occur directly
from irradiation? What is the driving force in the absence of a mechanical load to
initiate the transformation?
REPLY: According to the results of high-resolution STEM observations and MD
simulations, we inferred that the martensitic transformation occurs mostly due to the
interactions between pre-existing SFs and radiation-induced defects in irradiated GNS
304NG. As shown in Figs. 3(b, c) and Supplementary Fig. 21(c, d) in the revised
manuscript, the martensitic phase transition occurs mainly at the junctions of SFs after
irradiation, which conforms to the classical Kurdjumov-Sachs relationship. And further
MD simulations indicated that the phase transition is initiated while the radiation-
induced defects are absorbed by the SFs (Supplementary Video 4), confirming that the
radiation induced phase transformation is firstly induced by the interaction between SFs
and radiation-induced defects. And the mechanism of large-scale AMT was also
analyzed by building a MD model (Supplementary Fig. 25a) with cross SFs around the
newly formed martensite phase. Under the interaction of SFs and radiation-induced
defects, the phenomenon that martensite extends along these interactions to both sides
(Supplementary Fig. 25b, Supplementary Video 5) is confirmed. By analyzing the
displacement of interstitial atoms, it is found that the displacement of defects near the
interface between SFs and martensite is more significant, and finally martensite occurs
at the intersection of SFs and extends to both sides (Supplementary Fig. 25c).
Meanwhile, the corresponding phase transformation also promotes atomic
displacements after the formation of new martensite phase, resulting in continuous
martensitic transformation and related defect absorption from the damage peak to the
surrounding regions.
It is noted that the application of external stress is just to accelerate the phase
transformation process without affecting the underlying mechanism during MD
simulations in this work, although inhomogeneous stress fields do exist in irradiated
samples induced by implantation of energetic particles [20]. For example, a previous
study [20] demonstrated that the ion implantation could result in concentration gradient
and stress fields in the near-surface layer, and the maximum value could reach several
hundred MPa. Furthermore, displacement cascades and the formation of radiation
defects would also induce inhomogeneous stress fields around these regions [21].
Correspondingly, the driving force of martensitic transformation in irradiated GNS
samples mostly comes from the excess free energies relating with the pre-existing SFs
and radiation-induced defects. Meanwhile, the residual stresses introduced by SMRT,
phase transition, chemical segregation under irradiation and energetic particle
irradiation, might also provide additional driving force. And their contributions have
been discussed in the manuscript (see P10 Lines 273-277, Lines 302-307).
Some other changes have also been made to further clarify the AMT mechanism in the
revised manuscript (see P10 Lines 273-274, Lines 280-284, and Supplementary Note
1).
8. P8 Line 218: What does adaptive martensitic transformation mean, and how is this
different from a standard martensitic transformation?
REPLY: According to experimental and simulative results in this work, we found that
the martensitic transformation in irradiated GNS 304NG samples occurs much faster
and in a broader region than that a standard martensitic transformation in irradiated
coarse-grained counterparts. Therefore, we proposed the adaptive martensitic
transformation (AMT) to name the martensitic transformation process in GNS samples
under irradiation.
In detail, the AMT mechanism shows different features from the standard martensitic
transformation: 1) The AMT completes in a much lower dose in the peak damage region
of GNS samples than a standard martensitic transformation under irradiation at room
temperature without the application of external stress. The AMT results in a full
distribution of martensite in the peak damage region after irradiation at 12 dpa; while a
large fraction of austenite retains in the peak damage region after a standard martensitic
transformation even at 155 dpa. 2) The AMT progresses adaptively from the peak
damage region to the surrounding regions; while a standard martensitic transformation
occurs only in the peak damage region. 3) The AMT can occur at high temperatures
(e.g. 450 C) when no standard martensitic transformation can occur.
Corresponding changes have been made in the revised manuscript (P8 Line 221; Lines
240-243).

The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic
Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation
demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and
voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. 
Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive

REPLY：Thank you for the positive comments and insightful suggestions.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect,
shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the
martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual
stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT
mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a

martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
REPLY: Yes. We have analyzed the relationship between martensitic transformation
and residual stress in GNS samples under irradiation in this work.
Residual stress might play an important role in martensitic transformation in austenitic
steels, TRIP steels, shape memory alloys, et al. Typically, compressive stresses promote
martensitic transformation by decreasing the energy barrier of transformation. Since
higher compressive residual stresses exist in SMRT 304NG samples than in CG
samples, the AMT process might be further promoted in addition to the contribution of
SFs in GNS samples under irradiation at room temperature. In this work, the role of
residual stress on martensitic transformation has also been revealed by MD simulations,
in which remarkable stresses were introduced so that the martensitic transformation was
accelerated in an austenitic unit (see Supplementary Fig. 21). Meanwhile, it is noticed
that the large-scale AMT and enhanced irradiation resistance have also been observed
in GNS sample irradiated at higher temperatures (see Supplementary Fig. 10), when the
residual stresses are almost completely released. Therefore, it should be SFs play the
dominant role in the AMT process in this work. However, further investigations are
expected to clarify the effect of residual stress on the AMT under irradiation at room
temperature.
Meanwhile, we have measured the residual stresses in the surface layer of GNS and CG
samples before and after irradiation at room temperature. As shown in Fig. R4, a certain

increased (from -131.215.4 MPa to -182.610.7 MPa), while there is no detectable

relating with TRIP (transformation induced plasticity) effect, and therefore radiation
might bring significant changes in TRIP materials. For example, Agrawal et al. [1]
found that radiation might initiate a self-healing mechanism in TRIP high entropy alloys
(HEAs) by balancing radiation induced martensitic transformation with temperature
induced reverse transformation, so that a high stability of mechanical properties is
achieved in HEAs under irradiation at high doses and temperatures. And the self-
healing mechanism might be introduced to expand the service dose and temperature of

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This work provides interesting results concerning radiation tolerance improvements via surface treatment. The ion irradiation is an acceptable starting point for further investigation of radiation effects in this unique microstructure. Generally the conclusions are supported by the data, and the experimental and computation methods are sound. However, additional detail and explanation of certain concepts is suggested. This work is recommended for minor revision, then publication pending that revision.

### Reviewer 2

The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be addressed.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect, shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
2. The manuscript claims that the AMT mechanism is related to high-density SFs. So, what is the value of it. A detailed value would be appreciated.
3. The authors focus on studying the microstructure of the peak damage region. According to the dose and ion distribution map provided in Supplementary Fig. 3, the irradiation dose and ion concentration in the peak damage area are much higher than other irradiation regions. So, will this affect the martensitic transformation in this work?
4. In lines 105-106, the authors mention a 3D dislocation network was formed in 304NG by SMRT. That’s interesting. However, there seems to be no experimental evidence, and only been demonstrated through MD simulations.
5. In lines 141-143, “it is interesting to notice that both the density and size of DLs significantly decrease……0.5 to 5 dpa……” the range of the dose is incorrect (refer to Supplementary Fig. 4).

and used as plates of core shroud, core supporting structures, pipes in jet pumps and so

To understand and improve their radiation resistance would thus be useful and

temperature effect, we have proved that this mechanism still works well at temperature

receives a high dose and/or a high dose rate at temperatures at least up to 450 C.

radiation-induced displacement damages (mostly vacancies, interstitials, and their

nanocrystal samples, the density of above mentioned structures (grain boundaries,

vacancy clusters by lattice rearrangement during the AMT process, as revealed by the
present MD simulation results (Supplementary Video 4). Therefore, the total number of
vacancies and small vacancy clusters in both austenite and the transformed martensite
to form a void is further decreased by AMT process.

irradiation, which conforms to the classical Kurdjumov-Sachs relationship. And further

induced defects are absorbed by the SFs (Supplementary Video 4), confirming that the

and radiation-induced defects. And the mechanism of large-scale AMT was also
analyzed by building a MD model (Supplementary Fig. 25a) with cross SFs around the

displacement of interstitial atoms, it is found that the displacement of defects near the

Meanwhile, the corresponding phase transformation also promotes atomic
displacements after the formation of new martensite phase, resulting in continuous

surrounding regions.
It is noted that the application of external stress is just to accelerate the phase
transformation process without affecting the underlying mechanism during MD
simulations in this work, although inhomogeneous stress fields do exist in irradiated

study [20] demonstrated that the ion implantation could result in concentration gradient
and stress fields in the near-surface layer, and the maximum value could reach several
hundred MPa. Furthermore, displacement cascades and the formation of radiation
defects would also induce inhomogeneous stress fields around these regions [21].
Correspondingly, the driving force of martensitic transformation in irradiated GNS
samples mostly comes from the excess free energies relating with the pre-existing SFs
and radiation-induced defects. Meanwhile, the residual stresses introduced by SMRT,

irradiation, might also provide additional driving force. And their contributions have

transformation even at 155 dpa. 2) The AMT progresses adaptively from the peak
damage region to the surrounding regions; while a standard martensitic transformation
occurs only in the peak damage region. 3) The AMT can occur at high temperatures
(e.g. 450 C) when no standard martensitic transformation can occur.

Reviewer #2:
The draft “Extraordinary Radiation Resistance in Metals via Adaptive Martensitic
Transformation” by authors presents the findings of an experimental investigation
demonstrating the formation of unexpectedly lower densities of dislocation loops and
voids in a designed nanocrystalline austenitic stainless steel under ion irradiation. 
Accordingly, they find that a novel and interesting mechanism called adaptive
martensitic transformation (AMT) contributes to the superior radiation resistance. And
they further clarify and confirm the findings using MD simulations. Meanwhile, they
also find superior mechanical properties in the irradiated nanocrystalline samples.
The experimental design is reasonable. The microscopy studies are thorough and the
mechanical measurements are credible. And the process to produce the designed
nanocrystalline structure for AMT in mm-scale thicknesses at low cost is desirable. In
the referee’s opinion, this draft can be accepted for publication after several issues be
addressed.
REPLY：Thank you for the positive comments and insightful suggestions.
1. Martensitic transformation is a topic worthy of in-depth research, such as TRIP effect,
shape memory alloys, magnetism, etc. Residual stress has a significant impact on the
martensitic transformation. Although the authors mentioned the release of residual
stress at high temperatures in the line 261-267, the effect of residual stress on the AMT
mechanism at room temperature deserves further investigation and may become a
means of surface modification. Do the authors pay attention to the relationship between
martensitic transformation and residual stress in the irradiation samples?
REPLY: Yes. We have analyzed the relationship between martensitic transformation
and residual stress in GNS samples under irradiation in this work.
Residual stress might play an important role in martensitic transformation in austenitic
steels, TRIP steels, shape memory alloys, et al. Typically, compressive stresses promote
martensitic transformation by decreasing the energy barrier of transformation. Since
higher compressive residual stresses exist in SMRT 304NG samples than in CG
samples, the AMT process might be further promoted in addition to the contribution of
SFs in GNS samples under irradiation at room temperature. In this work, the role of
residual stress on martensitic transformation has also been revealed by MD simulations,
in which remarkable stresses were introduced so that the martensitic transformation was
accelerated in an austenitic unit (see Supplementary Fig. 21). Meanwhile, it is noticed
that the large-scale AMT and enhanced irradiation resistance have also been observed
in GNS sample irradiated at higher temperatures (see Supplementary Fig. 10), when the
residual stresses are almost completely released. Therefore, it should be SFs play the
dominant role in the AMT process in this work. However, further investigations are
expected to clarify the effect of residual stress on the AMT under irradiation at room
temperature.
Meanwhile, we have measured the residual stresses in the surface layer of GNS and CG
samples before and after irradiation at room temperature. As shown in Fig. R4, a certain
amount of compressive stress was introduced into the surface layer of 304NG samples
by SMRT. As the AMT progresses, the residual compressive stress was further
increased (from -131.215.4 MPa to -182.610.7 MPa), while there is no detectable
change in the residual stress in irradiated CG counterparts.
In addition, as pointed by the reviewer, martensitic transformation is also an issue
relating with TRIP (transformation induced plasticity) effect, and therefore radiation
might bring significant changes in TRIP materials. For example, Agrawal et al. [1]
found that radiation might initiate a self-healing mechanism in TRIP high entropy alloys
(HEAs) by balancing radiation induced martensitic transformation with temperature
induced reverse transformation, so that a high stability of mechanical properties is
achieved in HEAs under irradiation at high doses and temperatures. And the self-
healing mechanism might be introduced to expand the service dose and temperature of
TRIP HEAs in future reactors.
Corresponding modifications have been made in the revised manuscript (P10 Lines
302-307 on residual stress; P2 Lines 65-69, P9 Line 268 and P13 Line 376 on TRIP
effect).

The contributions of low energy interfaces (e.g. Σ3 (111) GBs), SFs and DNs to the

typically very stable under heating or irradiation mostly due to their low stored energies

which contribute to the high microstructure stability from a thermodynamic aspect.

annihilate the radiation induced defects inside grains. This should decrease the defects
absorption at GBs and therefore reduce GB migration under irradiation. Therefore, the
existence of a massive pre-formed SFs also contributes to microstructure stability.

interfacial Lomer-Cottrell locks, junctions, and so on [3]. Therefore, such a special
microstructure (combining low energy interfaces, SFs, and DNs) contributes to a high
stability from both thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives. And the grain size is still
within nanometer scale after irradiation at a very high dose or at a high temperature.
